name: Thailand Lisu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hope, Edward R. 1973. Selected phonological rules for Thailand Lisu. In Papers in South East Asian Linguistics No. 3, 19-34. Pacific Linguistics A-30. Canberra: Australian National University. doi:10.15144/PL-A30.19 (CC BY-SA 2015 online edition).
catalog_locator: p. 29, section 3 'Phonological rules', A 'Pre-cycle rules', (a) 'Stress assignment'; tone statement p. 22, section 'Non-consonants'.
catalog_quote: The assignment of primary stress is difficult to state without a detailed explanation of the syntactic component of Lisu grammar. Surface strings from that component are assigned linear order by topicalisation and focus rules (see Hope 1972) and primary stress is assigned to the main verb if it is not part of the major presupposition of the sentence, and to the head of the focus NP if the main verb is presupposed. ... In (1) where the stress is on tha 'here' the sentence would be the answer to the question 'Where is Asa?'. In (2) where the stress is on tya 'is' the sentence would be the answer to the question 'What is Asa doing?'. Secondary stress is assigned to the first syllable of the head noun of the component NPs and of the head verb of the sentence if these have not already received primary stress. Tertiary stress is assigned to syntactic markers. In the case of bi-syllabic markers the syllable to be stressed is specified by the output of the syntactic component.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Lisu; this is the first explicit stress statement found for the language. It supplies a placement rule at the sentence level (main verb / focus NP head) with secondary and tertiary levels, and says nothing about a fixed word-level position. The other nine Lisu works checked earlier (Hope 1971, Hope 1974, Bradley 1994, Bradley et al. 2006, Yu 2007, Tabain et al. 2019, Stanley 2023, Fraser 1922, Li 2017) are silent on placement, so nothing on record contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in (Thailand/Southern) Lisu is assigned by the syntax at sentence level, not by a word-level rule: primary stress goes to the main verb unless the verb is presupposed, in which case it goes to the head of the focus NP (the paper's examples 1-2 show the same string 'Asa is here' stressed on 'here' vs on 'is' depending on the question answered). Secondary stress goes to the first syllable of the head noun of each NP and of the head verb if not already primary-stressed; tertiary stress goes to grammatical markers. Tone is a property of every syllable (p. 22: 'All syllabic segments will be specified for tone.. syllables rather than segments are distinguished by tone'), so the language is tonal with a focus-driven stress overlay.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the head noun of the component NPs and of the head verb of the sentence when these lack primary stress; tertiary stress on syntactic markers, with the stressed syllable of bisyllabic markers set by the syntactic component (p. 29).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says primary-stress assignment cannot be fully stated without the syntactic component (Hope 1972). The Hope 1971 companion paper (PL-A29.53, already held by the project) mentions 'unstressed syllables' (p. 58) and 'other than primary stress' (pp. 62-63) as conditioning allophony and nasalisation loss, consistent with this multi-level stress system.
new_statements.identity_note: Hope 1973 describes Thailand Lisu, i.e. the Southern dialect (Hope's own fieldwork; the same variety as Hope 1971 and Bradley et al. 2006). Northern Lisu (Bradley 1994, Stanley 2023) and Central Lisu (Fraser 1922, Tabain et al. 2019) sources held by the project are silent on stress, so the sentence-level stress statement is attested for Southern Lisu only.

tone_statements.citation: Stanley, Rael, Marija Tabain, David Bradley & Defen Yu. 2023. Northern Lisu vowels & tones, and their interactions. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 154(4_supplement): A77 (186th ASA meeting abstract). doi:10.1121/10.0022854
tone_statements.quote: Northern Lisu has six tones, including four modal and two creaky-voiced tones; it has ten vowels, including five front vowels, four back vowels, and a central “fricative” vowel. Tone and vowel interaction is analyzed using Esling’s Laryngeal Articulator Model. Results show all speakers produce a lower f0 in the retracted vowel context, but it is not the case that all tones are creakier in this same vowel context.

tone_statements.translation: This idea rests on the fact that the correspondences, especially the tone correspondences, between Kunming Chinese and Lisu agree quite clearly. The four tones of Pekingese take, in Kunming, the values listed on the left below; each of these tone types is received in Lisu as the type listed on its right: Chinese 1. Yinping, Kunming 33 -> Lisu mid-level type; 2. Yangping 31 -> low-level type; 3. Shang 53 -> low-level type; 4. Qu 13 -> rising type or high-level type.

sources.citation: Hope, Edward R. 1974. The deep syntax of Lisu sentences: a transformational case grammar. Pacific Linguistics B-34. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-B34
sources.note: Orthography/phonology note pp. vi-viii: suprasegmentals posited are palatalisation, labialisation, laryngealisation and five tones; stress not listed. p.12: in Lisu focus is marked by linear order, whereas in English phonological stress marks focus. p.155: 'a morphophonemic rule adds stress to the particular verb.. being negated' (contrastive/sentence level). sources.citation: Hope, Edward R. 1971. Problems of phone assignment in the description of Thailand Lisu phonology. In W. Glover, M. Hari & E. R. Hope (eds), Papers in South East Asian Linguistics No. 2, 53-78. Pacific Linguistics A-29. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-A29.53
sources.note: Southern (Thailand) Lisu. Sec. 4 'Problems of assignment of suprasegmentals' covers tone and laryngealisation only. Stress appears only in passing: p.58 an on-glide allophone of /zY/ is the only one 'in all unstressed syllables'; pp.62-63 nasalisation of [h]-initial syllables tends to disappear 'in syllables with mid tone when these have other than primary stress'. No statement of where stress falls.
